claims.text: Adding vanadium to CoCrFeNi will drive a transformation toward a bcc-type solid solution.
The vanadium-induced bcc solid solution will be more homogeneous than the baseline microstructure.
Vanadium addition will reduce elemental segregation and phase inhomogeneity in CoCrFeNi.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy is likely multiphase with an fcc-dominant microstructure.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has moderate hardness.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has moderate wear resistance.
A vanadium concentration on the order of 0.5 atomic fraction is proposed for the modified CoCrFeNi alloy.
Formation of the vanadium-containing solid solution will increase hardness.
The modified alloy will maintain stabilized hardness from room temperature to 800 °C.
The harder solid solution will reduce localized deformation during sliding.
Vanadium may promote protective, high-temperature-stable oxides at the sliding interface.
The modified alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi at room temperature.
The modified alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi at elevated temperatures up to 800 °C.
The modified alloy will have a lower wear rate than unmodified CoCrFeNi at room temperature.
The modified alloy will have a lower wear rate than unmodified CoCrFeNi at elevated temperatures up to 800 °C.
The proposed comparison is limited to sliding in air from room temperature to 800 °C under matched load and sliding-speed conditions.
Performance in corrosive or vacuum environments is outside the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as a 'small amount' and as 'microalloying,' but 0.5 atomic fraction literally means 50 at.% V, which is a major compositional replacement rather than a microalloying addition. The cited Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 notation instead uses a relative formula coefficient and does not establish 50 at.% V.
